title: Rosh Hashanah: the boy is heard (Genesis 21)
hookLine: the first day's reading includes Hagar and Ishmael rescued by a well

cards: The desert of Beer-sheba. A woman and her son, sent away from the only home he's known with some bread and a skin of water. The water runs out.
The boy weakens. His mother lays him under one of the bushes, walks away about a bowshot, and sits down. She can't watch him die.
She lifts up her voice and weeps. On the first morning of Rosh Hashanah, this is the story read aloud from the Torah.

teach.b: Genesis 21 begins with joy: Sarah, at last, gives birth to Isaac. The Talmud links that to Rosh Hashanah too: Sarah was remembered on this day. But the reading doesn't stop at the happy ending.
It goes on to Hagar, Sarah's servant, and her son Ishmael, Abraham's firstborn, sent away into the wilderness.

Then comes the verse at the center: "And God heard the voice of the lad; and the angel of God called to Hagar out of heaven, and said unto her: 'What aileth thee, Hagar? fear not; for God hath heard the voice of the lad where he is.'" It's Hagar who weeps aloud, but the verse says God heard the boy, maybe his own quiet cry.
And Ishmael's name means God hears, given before he was born, when Hagar first fled into the desert.

Then God opens her eyes, and she sees a well of water she hadn't seen. The rabbis lingered on the words where he is. Rashi, drawing on the midrash, says the angels objected: this boy's descendants will one day cause harm.
God answered: what is he right now? Right now, he's innocent. A person is judged as they are, where they are, today.
On the day of judgment, that's the reading: not who you might become, not what your children might do. Ishmael is honored in Muslim tradition as well, as a prophet and an ancestor.
Here, in the Jewish reading, he is simply a thirsty boy, and he is heard.

how: On the first day of Rosh Hashanah, Genesis 21, Isaac's birth and the rescue of Hagar and Ishmael, is read from the Torah scroll in the synagogue; the second day reads Genesis 22, the binding of Isaac.

games.q: in the midrash, the angels object: this boy's descendants will cause harm, so why save him? what does God answer?
o: what is he right now? judge him where he is.
his father Abraham earned it for him.
games.why: God judges him as he is today: innocent, thirsty, and heard.

practice: Think of someone outside your circle you don't usually think about, someone sent away, someone on the other side of a line, someone whose story isn't yours, and picture them where they are right now: thirsty, tired, or just living their day.
If you pray, ask God to hear them, as the boy was heard; if not, wish them a well of water, whatever that means for them.
